description: I’m Mohamed Mostafa, a STEM Fayoum student and developer passionate about AI, web development, data visualization, computer vision, and interactive experiences. I’ve participated in ISEF, NASA Space Apps, Purple Comet, IEEE IC-SIT, and DECI. I’m looking for teammates in AI/ML, data science, Earth/space science, UI/UX, research, 3D visualization, or storytelling. Let’s build!
summary: Earth Guardian AI answers the challenge “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots”. NASA’s MODIS (1 km pixels) and VIIRS (375 m pixels) detect the same wildfires at different times, sizes and confidence scales, so one fire can appear twice and results are different most of the time. Our web app merges both sensors’ live NASA FIRMS detections, matches those within about 1.2 km, and gives every hotspot one harmonized confidence score from 0 to 100. The hotspots appear on an interactive 3D NASA globe with a sensor-agreement panel, grouped fire events and a wind-direction arrow from NASA POWER. The app also gives a wildfire risk score for any place, a what-if simulator and an AI assistant with voice in 20 languages, including Egyptian Arabic, so people can understand fire danger in their own language.
details:
What it does. Earth Guardian AI is a browser-based 3D globe for live wildfire monitoring. It harmonizes NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into one deduplicated list with a single 0 to 100 confidence score, shows where the sensors agree, estimates local wildfire risk from NASA weather data, and explains results in plain language in 20 languages.

How it works.

  1. The server downloads near-real-time detections from NASA FIRMS (VIIRS SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and MODIS) for the area on screen.
  2. Each VIIRS detection is matched to the nearest MODIS detection within about 0.012 degrees (about 1.2 km). A matched pair becomes one fire. Unmatched detections stay as single-sensor fires.
  3. Confidence is normalized to 0..1 (VIIRS l/n/h = 0.2/0.6/1.0, MODIS 0..100 divided by 100).
  4. Harmonized score (max 100) = agreement (45 if both sensors, 10 if one) + sensor confidence (up to 25) + fire radiative power (up to 15) + closeness of the two detections (up to 15). Label: HIGH = both sensors, MEDIUM = one confident sensor, LOW otherwise.
  5. Extra products: fire events (nearby detections grouped), a persistent-hotspot flag (same cell on 2 or more days, for example industrial heat sources), age of each detection, and agreement statistics for the view.
  6. A wildfire risk score (0 to 100) uses NASA POWER temperature, humidity, rainfall, soil moisture and wind, plus nearby harmonized fires. It is a simplified index inspired by the Canadian Fire Weather Index (Van Wagner, 1987), not the full operational system.
  7. NASA GIBS thermal-anomaly layers are shown under the dots as a visual cross-check.

Benefits. One trusted fire layer instead of two confusing ones; transparent scoring (every point is explained); faster understanding of which fires are real and strong; access in the user's own language, including Egyptian Arabic, by text or voice.

What we hope to achieve. Make satellite fire information easier to trust and to understand for the public and for early responders, and show how MODIS and VIIRS together are better than either alone (VIIRS finds many small fires MODIS misses; MODIS adds a longer-heritage confirmation).

Limitations (stated openly). Satellites pass only a few times a day, so detections can be hours old and small or short fires can be missed. NASA POWER weather lags real time by a few days. The risk index is simplified. The 1.2 km matching distance follows the MODIS pixel size and has not been validated against ground-truth fire perimeters. In the 10-year chart the past bars are a modelled reconstruction (not measured history) and the future bars are scenarios, not predictions. Translations other than English and Arabic are AI-generated. Not for emergency decisions.

Tools, languages and software. TypeScript, Next.js 16 (React), Tailwind CSS, CesiumJS with Resium (3D globe), Node.js server routes, Groq API for language models (assistant, explanations, translation), Web Speech API (voice), SVG charts. Data scripts in Node/TypeScript. Open-source packages from npm.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes. We used SI in two ways, and we are clearly identifying both.

  1. During development: an AI coding assistant helped us write and debug much of the code (TypeScript/React/Next.js, API routes, the harmonization and risk functions, the data-preparation scripts) and parts of the text and documentation. Our team chose the challenge and the design, directed the work, tested the application and reported and decided every change, and we take responsibility for the result. AI-assisted parts are code, descriptive text and documentation; no images, audio or video in the project were generated by AI, and the project contains no NASA logos or mission identifiers that we modified.
  2. Inside the product at run time: the app calls Groq-hosted large language models for the AI assistant (chat and voice), the plain-language "why this risk / why this confidence" explanations, and on-demand translation into 20 languages. These outputs are generated text from the model and are not NASA content. The numeric scores themselves come from deterministic code in lib/fireHarmonize.ts and lib/riskEngine.ts, not from the language model.
